newsitem.title: USA: Policy should follow, not fight cycles--Fed expert.
newsitem.headline: Policy should follow, not fight cycles--Fed expert.

text.p: The Federal Reserve's monetary policy should be pegged to the nominal funds rate and follow -- not fight -- business cycles, a Cleveland Fed economist said on Tuesday.

"Inflation, in the long-run, will really be due to what the Fed does," Cleveland Fed economist Charles Carlstrom told Reuters. "Pegging the nominal fed funds rate implies what the long-term inflation rate is going to be. Inflation is going to be pinned down by the federal funds rate."

Carlstom also said the Fed should add liquidity during expansions or withdraw liquidity during recessions to keep the funds rate constant regardless of the business cycle -- much in the same way it satisfies daily demand for bank reserves.

"An elastic currency, by supplying additional liquidity in booms and withdrawing it in recessions, allows investment and employment to respond more quickly and efficiently to the shocks that buffet the economy," Carlstrom noted.
He described an elastic currency as one "that could be quickly expanded or contracted as needed."
Carlstrom co-authored a paper on the issue with Timothy Fuerst, associate professor of economics at Bowling Green State University.

The Cleveland Fed economist questioned why the Fed is pro-cyclical -- or meets demands for reserves on a seasonal basis -- while it is counter-cyclical during the business cycle, trying to "lean against the wind" to either curb or stimulate economic growth.
Carlstrom noted demand for liquidity are essentially similar in seasonal and business cycles alike.
"Counter-cyclical money may smooth output and, potentially, even consumption," Carlstrom said. "But that has little to no effect on real variables, real output and real interest rates."
Carlstrom acknowledged his theory can be criticized as advocating a policy that may result in periods of inflation.

"A related argument against pegging nominal interest rates is that procyclical money growth would exacerbate business cycle fluctuations. Cyclical swings would be wider than with a 'lean-against-the-wind' policy," Carlstrom said.
"This highlights why it is so important that the central bank has the credibility necessary to maintain an interest rate peg," Carlstom stressed.
Carlstrom predicted a pro-cyclical monetary policy would result in wider real sector and inflation swings.
The benefit, however, would be that consumption would run at a higher pace, he added.

"Average consumption would quite likely be higher in a world where the Fed holds the funds rate constant. Individuals would therefore be better off with an interest rate peg, even though consumption and short-term inflation would both be more variable," the Cleveland Fed economist forecast.
However, Carlstrom cautioned a pro-cyclical monetary policy could not be implemented unless the Fed achieves a greater level of credibility than it now enjoys.
"We do believe there are sound economic reasons why the central bank should let the money supply vary positively with out," he concluded.
